newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Kabila's Congo discusses security with Angola.
newsitem.headline: Kabila's Congo discusses security with Angola.

text.p: The Democratic Republic of the Congo said on Friday it was discussing security matters with Angola, which backed the rebellion to topple Mobutu Sese Seko but now faces a growing threat from its own opponents.
"We and Angola have a border of 2,600 km (1,600 miles) so you would understand we have so much to discuss together," Kinshasa's Foreign Minister Bizima Karaha told a news conference in Pretoria.
"There is no way that we cannot discuss security," he added when asked about a visit this week to Angola by Congo's President Laurent Kabila.
Kabila, who toppled president Mobutu Sese Seko of what was Zaire in May, had two days of talks in the Angolan capital Luanda this week with President Jose Eduardo dos Santos.

There was no official word on whether they had discussed military cooperation but diplomats said dos Santos was likely to have asked Kabila to play a vital role in helping the Angolan government deal with former rebel movement UNITA if hostilities resume.
A three-year-old peace accord between Jonas Savimbi's UNITA and dos Santos's MPLA is coming unstuck, diplomats say.
The two sides have clashed in the north, near the Congo border, in recent weeks, raising fears that a two-decade civil war that ended in 1994 could resume.
UNITA is widely believed to have sent troops to help Mobutu, to repay him for support during Angola's war and afterwards.

The former rebels, who still control much of Angola's countryside and diamond mines, sent gems -- which helped bankroll their movement -- out of the country through Zaire for sale. Mobutu's fall has closed this route.

Karaha said Congo hoped the 1994 Angolan peace deal, signed in Zambia's capital Lusaka, would not unravel. But he declined to rule out military support from Kabila's alliance forces if civil war resumed in its southern neighbour.
"We fully support the Lusaka accord. We do not support the military option," he said after talks with South African Foreign Minister Alfred Nzo.
"We will do everything we can so that war won't resume."
Karaha said he was in South Africa to thank President Nelson Mandela for his diplomatic help and to tell the country there was still much it could do to reconstruct the former Zaire.
"The people of South Africa, and especially the business community, can help in rebuilding our country," he said.
Nzo said Mandela had invited Kabila to visit South Africa, probably within the next few weeks.
